description: Structured geography of the Mayhew extract. Coords are modern WGS84 (lat, lng) approximations of 1851 locations — use them to place map pins but cite source.txt for any historical claim. chapter_refs and character_refs point to the canonical /api/chapters and /api/characters ids.

entries.name: Cuckold's Point
entries.description: Bend on the Rotherhithe side of the Thames, eastern anchor of the tosher's working shore. Where the shore-worker's first memory is — sinking in mud up to his knees until rescued. Named for a medieval stake-and-horns marker said to indicate Edward II's gift of cuckoldry-shaming rights to the miller.

entries.name: Blackfriars Bridge (city sewer mouth)
entries.description: The city sewer outlet the toshers worked until it was boarded up. Trespass penalty by the tosher's time was fourteen days: "if you was caught up it and brought afore the Lord Mayor, he'd give you fourteen days on it."

entries.name: Bishop Bonner's Fields
entries.description: Open ground in Bethnal Green where fifty-year-old cellar rubbish was shot in two loads — the tosher worked both alone and made £3 5s, finding a gold chain he first took for copper. Named for Edmund Bonner, the Marian Bishop of London.

entries.name: Hyde Park (Parliament Houses fire rubbish, 1834)
entries.description: After the Parliament Houses burned on 16 October 1834 the rubbish was shot in Hyde Park. The Cuckold's Point tosher and his mate Long J—— worked it for months, making £3+ each per day: sovereigns, half-sovereigns, silver half-melted, jewellery, rings, stones, brooches. Their quarrel over the split ended their access and the remaining rubbish was buried.

entries.name: Petticoat Lane (Middlesex Street) & Rag Fair
entries.description: Headquarters of the bone-grubbers and a market for toshers' stolen or salvaged metals. The Petticoat-lane Jew fence paid £7 10s for bracelets the tosher first took to a jeweller who tested them as only plated. Heart of the East-end rag-and-old-clothes trade.

entries.name: Bermondsey Tanyards
entries.description: Cluster of London tanyards south of the Thames — the pure-finders' only market. Named yards in Mayhew: Leomont & Roberts, Bavingtons, Beech, Murrell, Cheeseman, Powell, Jones, Jourdans, Kent, Moorcroft, Davis. The alkaline ammonia in 'pure' (dogs' dung) was used to finish morocco and kid leather.

entries.name: St Katharine Docks / Rosemary Lane district
entries.description: The "wretched locality" between the London and St Katharine's Docks and Rosemary Lane — tumbled houses, dust-heaps, ragged children, headquarters of the bone-grubbers.

entries.name: Ratcliffe Highway
entries.description: Eastern dockland high-street — beat of the destitute Irish cigar-end finders. Also J.C.'s school neighbourhood: Red Lion School at Green-bank, near Old Gravel-lane.

entries.name: Ragged School, High Street, Wapping
entries.description: J.C.'s gang headquarters — the Ragged School at Wapping where the 14-year-old mud-lark was rescued from the Old Gravel-lane gang (C—— the 18-year-old captain, B—— B——, B—— L——, W—— B——, Tim) and placed as an apprentice at Bradbury & Evans.

entries.name: King James's Stairs, Wapping Wall
entries.description: Central Thames access point for the mud-larks of Shadwell and Wapping — where Mayhew watched them on the foreshore at low tide.

entries.name: Whitechapel Workhouse Hospital
entries.description: Where the Liverpool-Irish bone-grubber spent nine weeks one winter, sick and destitute after his railway-savings fraud.

entries.name: Thames foreshore — Shadwell & Wapping side
entries.description: The barefoot-mud-larks' working shore. Coal, copper nails, rope, bones gathered at low tide. Shared with the shore-men (toshers) who take the sewer outlets here too.
